guide.title: Fairfield, Connecticut: Burned in 1779, Rebuilt on the Green
guide.intro: Roger Ludlow, a framer of Connecticut's Fundamental Orders, bought land from the Pequonnock Indians in 1639 and laid out four "squares" divided by five roadways — a plan that survives today as the Historic Town Green. English settlers called the coastal area, known to Native Americans as Uncoway, their "fair fields"; the Uncowas, Sasquas, Maxumux, and Pequonnocks, all Paugussett subdivisions, had lived along this shoreline before them, and in July 1637 the Great Swamp Fight — the Pequot War's final violent episode — took place in swampland near present-day Southport. The Revolution brought devastation: on July 8, 1779, British troops under General William Tryon burned more than two hundred buildings, and visiting a decade later, George Washington still noted "the chimneys of many burnt houses standing." Fairfield rebuilt, later ceding land to help form Westport, and in 1914 resident Mabel Osgood Wright founded the Birdcraft Sanctuary, one of the country's first private songbird refuges.

sections.heading: Four squares, a swamp fight, and a burning
sections.body: Fairfield's permanent settlement began in 1639, when Roger Ludlow — a framer of Connecticut's Fundamental Orders — purchased land from the Pequonnock Indians and laid out four "squares" divided by five roadways; that original center survives today as the Historic Town Green. The town's name comes from the "fair fields" English settlers found along the coast, an area Native Americans called Uncoway; the Uncowas, Sasquas, Maxumux, and Pequonnocks, subdivisions of the Paugussett people, inhabited the coastal areas before European settlement. In July 1637, the Great Swamp Fight — the final violent episode of the Pequot War — took place in swampland in the vicinity of Southport, now part of Fairfield. On July 8, 1779, British troops under General William Tryon landed and burned Fairfield; a rear guard of German mercenaries set fire to virtually all the buildings, including churches, destroying more than two hundred structures. Visiting in 1789, George Washington noted "the chimneys of many burnt houses standing" were still visible. Fairfield was one of the four earliest towns established in the Connecticut Colony, and portions of it were eventually annexed to form the town of Westport. In 1914, Fairfield writer and conservationist Mabel Osgood Wright, founder of the Connecticut Audubon Society, created the town's Birdcraft Sanctuary, one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States and now a National Historic Landmark.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Most visitors drive in on I-95 (Exit 22 for the historic town center) or the Merritt Parkway / Route 15 (Exit 44, Black Rock Turnpike), with US-1 (the Post Road) running through downtown. Metro-North's New Haven Line provides direct Grand Central-to-Fairfield service at three stations in town: Fairfield (165 Unquowa Road), Fairfield–Black Rock (formerly Fairfield Metro, 61 Constant Comment Way), and Southport (400 Center Street).

sections.heading: Beaches, a sanctuary, and a stage
sections.body: Birdcraft Museum & Sanctuary, founded in 1914 by Mabel Osgood Wright, is one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States and a National Historic Landmark, with more than 150 bird species recorded on its 5 acres; museum hours are Thursday, Saturday & Sunday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m., with trails open dawn to dusk year-round. Penfield Beach is one of Fairfield's town beaches on Long Island Sound, with non-resident daily parking during the beach season. The Fairfield Museum and History Center sits beside the Historic Town Green with free general admission through November 25, 2026, and its seasonal Ogden House & Gardens, a c. 1750 saltbox farmhouse, opens Sunday afternoons in summer. The Fairfield Theatre Company runs two indoor stages plus an outdoor stage for live music.

faq.question: How do I get to Fairfield?
faq.answer: Drivers use I-95 (Exit 22) or the Merritt Parkway/Route 15 (Exit 44), with US-1 through downtown. Metro-North's New Haven Line runs direct to Grand Central Terminal from three stations: Fairfield, Fairfield–Black Rock, and Southport.

faq.question: What is Birdcraft Sanctuary?
faq.answer: Founded in 1914 by Mabel Osgood Wright, it is one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States and a National Historic Landmark, with more than 150 species recorded on 5 acres. Free admission.

faq.question: How much is beach parking at Penfield Beach?
faq.answer: During the season (Memorial Day Saturday to Labor Day), non-resident daily parking is $40 on weekdays and $50 on weekends and holidays.

faq.question: What happened to Fairfield in 1779?
faq.answer: British troops under General William Tryon burned the town on July 8, 1779, destroying more than two hundred buildings; visiting a decade later, George Washington still noted the burnt chimneys standing.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Fairfield?
faq.answer: Delamar Southport, a boutique hotel in Southport's historic quarter, and The Circle Hotel Fairfield, on the Post Road near the beaches, are both verified in-town options.

places.name: Fairfield Museum and History Center
places.summary: A local history museum and research library beside the Historic Town Green; general admission is free from January 13 through November 25, 2026. Open Tuesday-Sunday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

places.name: Ogden House & Gardens
places.summary: A c. 1750 saltbox farmhouse operated by the Fairfield Museum, open seasonally 1-4 p.m. on Sundays from June through September, with the outdoor Dooryard Garden open year-round.

places.name: Birdcraft Museum & Sanctuary
places.summary: Founded in 1914 by Mabel Osgood Wright, Birdcraft is one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States and a National Historic Landmark; more than 150 bird species have been recorded on its 5 acres. Museum hours Thursday, Saturday & Sunday, 10 a.m.-3 p.m.; trails dawn to dusk, free.
places.history: Founded in 1914 by writer and conservationist Mabel Osgood Wright, founder of the Connecticut Audubon Society; one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States and now a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: Fairfield Theatre Company
places.summary: A nonprofit live-music and arts venue in downtown Fairfield with two indoor stages — the 225-capacity StageOne and the 640-capacity Warehouse — plus an outdoor stage, The Lot.

places.name: Penfield Beach
places.summary: One of Fairfield's town beaches on Long Island Sound. During the beach season (Memorial Day Saturday to Labor Day), non-residents can pay daily parking — $40 weekdays, $50 weekends/holidays.

places.name: Rawley's Drive-In
places.summary: A hot dog institution established in 1947, with testimonials from Martha Stewart and Alex Guarnaschelli. Open Monday-Saturday, 11 a.m.-7 p.m.; closed Sunday.

places.name: Archie Moore's Bar & Restaurant (Fairfield)
places.address: Sanford Street, Fairfield, CT (downtown, adjacent to the Fairfield train station)
places.summary: The Fairfield outpost of the Connecticut tavern founded on Willow Street in New Haven in 1898; this location opened in 1992 in a former printing warehouse with indoor and outdoor seating.

places.name: Pizzeria Molto
places.summary: A modern Italian restaurant on the Post Road emphasizing shared plates, handmade pastas, and an extensive cocktail and wine program.

places.name: Delamar Southport
places.summary: A boutique New England hotel in Southport's historic quarter (a village within the town of Fairfield), with the on-site Artisan restaurant, a private spa, and complimentary breakfast.

places.name: The Circle Hotel Fairfield
places.summary: A boutique coastal-inspired hotel on the Post Road near Fairfield's beaches and universities, offering free breakfast, a seasonal outdoor pool, seasonal beach passes, and free bike rentals for direct bookings.
